01 WHO IS AUDEMARS
PIGUET?
Audemars Piguet is a Swiss fine watchmaking house, based in Le Brassus, which was founded
in Vallé de Joux in 1875 by Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet under the name
“Audemars Piguet & Cie”, completes together with Patek Philippe and Vacheron Constantin the
“Holy Trinity” from Swiss watchmaking.
These two men were watchmakers, Audemars created several extremely
complexes for brands such as “Tiffany&Co” while Piguet specialized in regulating
movements.
When the brand began its activity, responsibility was divided in such a way as to entrust
Audemars handled production and technical development while Piguet handled management and sales.
Since its foundation, this brand has been in the “hands” of the same families (The Audemars family
and the Piguet Family).
Audemars Piguet (AP) has been a major influence on luxury watchmaking since its inception.
its founding in 1875 and continues to shape the industry with constant innovation both in terms
design and in technical terms. The brand has contributed significantly to shaping the
luxury watch industry with some notable innovations.
They are:
➢ 1892: Created the first minute repeating movement for wristwatches, which
it was later sold to Louis Brandt frères (Omega SA).
➢ 1899: Manufactured a "Grand Complication" pocket watch with seven complications,
including “grand strike” and “small strike”, minute repeater”, alarm, “perpetual calendar”,
“deadbeat seconds”, “chronoograph with jumping seconds” and a “split seconds hand”.
➢ 1921: Created the first “jumping-hour” wristwatch, powered by the Caliber
HPVM10.
➢ 1934: Introduced the first “skeleton” watch.
➢ 1946: Produced the thinnest watch, with a 1.64 mm thick movement.
➢ 1972: Introduced the first “sportswatch” wristwatch, the “Royal Oak”.
➢ 1986: Created the ultra-thin automatic watch with tourbillon (Caliber 2870), measuring just 5.3
mm thick (including case).
➢ 1995/96: Manufactured the first automatic watch "Grand Complication" (Caliber 2885).
➢ 2006: Introduced the first direct impulse exhaust, based on a design from the
watchmaker Robert Robin, from the 18th century.
➢ 2007/08: Developed the first watch with a carbon case and carbon movement
(Royal Oak Carbon Concept).
➢ 2015: Launched the first mechanical chronograph with independent memory and three wheels
column, called “Royal Oak Concept Laptimer Michael Schumacher”.
➢ 2019: Introduced the world's thinnest automatic perpetual calendar.
02 BRAND AND ANALYSIS
COMPETITORS
AUDEMARS PIGUET SWOT ANALYSIS
Strengths
• Heritage and reputation: More than 140 years of history and recognized technical innovations.
• Constant innovation: Pioneering complications such as minute repeater, tourbillon
ultra-thin, direct impulse exhaust, among others.
• Extreme luxury positioning: High prices guarantee substantial margins.
• Iconic design: The Royal Oak and its variations are global references in sports luxury.
• Iconic collections:
the Royal Oak (1972): Revolutionized the industry by being the first sports watch
luxury steel with haute horlogerie finish. The octagonal design with
visible screws, signed by Gérald Genta, became an instant icon and
symbol of distinction.
the Royal Oak Offshore (1993): More robust and bold interpretation of the Royal Oak,
aimed at a younger and more daring audience. With large box,
innovative materials and imposing aesthetics, it has become a regular presence on the wrist
of athletes and celebrities.
o Code 11.59 by Audemars Piguet (2019): Introduction of a new language
aesthetics and watchmaking for the 21st century. With complex geometry box
multiple, lacquered or enamelled dials and new generation calibres, aims to
combining technical tradition with contemporary expression.
• Strong presence in pop culture: Partnerships with celebrities, athletes, musicians and in films
that increase brand recognition.
• Independent family business: Agile decision-making, long-term vision and
preservation of the brand’s DNA.
• Model exclusivity: Reduced catalog and limited production, reinforces the character
odd of each piece.
• Strong secondary market: High demand and appreciation in the “pre-owned” market,
confirm the robustness of “brand equity”.
• Royal Oak Innovation: Launch of the first luxury sports watch in 1972,
revolutionizing the watch industry.
Weaknesses
• Limited production: Low volume of parts produced per year, restricting the scale of
recipe.
• Environmental image: “Latecomers/Non-transparent” classification by WWF in 2018,
affects ESG reputation.
• Dependence on a niche: Very restricted target audience; sensitive to economic crises
luxury consumption.
• Controlled distribution channel: Few own points of sale, limiting the
penetration into new markets.
• Succession risk: Dependence on family governance processes can generate
uncertainties in generational transitions.
• Restricted scale: Annual production of around 40,000 units limits the potential for
revenue growth.
• Reduction in the use of traditional watches: The popularization of “smartphones” and
“Smartwatches” reduce the demand for traditional luxury watches.
Opportunities
• Expansion in emerging markets: China, Middle East and Latin America with strong
growth of ultra-luxury.
• Sustainability and transparency: Invest in green practices, certification of materials
raw materials (Fairmined, RJC) and ESG reports to improve the image.
• Customization and digital services: Offer online personalization, “after-market” experiences
sales” and virtual interaction platforms.
• Collaborations and limited editions: Partnerships with artists, designers and celebrities
expand appeal and reach.
• “Certified Pre-Owned” Program: Create or collaborate with official “pre-owned” platforms
owned” certified to capture additional revenue and retain new customers.
• “Gold-backed appeal”: With the price of gold at ≈€95/g, the intrinsic value of watches
in gold reinforces its appeal as a safe haven asset in high inflation environments.
• Strategic management of raw materials: Long-term partnerships with suppliers and use
of certified materials to ensure supply and reinforce ESG credibility.
• Hybrid innovations: Respond to the threat of “smartwatches” with models that integrate
technological features without losing the identity of the luxury watch.
Threats
• Fierce competition: Patek Philippe, Vacheron Constantin, Richard Mille and brands
Independents reinforce the dispute in the luxury market.
• Economic volatility: Recessions and exchange rate variations directly affect sales
of luxury.
• Global inflation: Rising costs of raw materials, energy and labor,
they put pressure on margins and customer purchasing power.
• Volatile raw materials: Price fluctuations and risks of shortages of precious metals
and minerals, can impact production costs and deadlines.
• Counterfeiting and “grey market”: Replicas and parallel resale can devalue the market
official.
• Behavior change: Younger generations may prioritize experiences and
services rather than the possession of material goods.
• Commercial tariffs and protectionist barriers: Imposition of
import/export that can increase costs, reduce margin and limit access to
markets.
• Increase in crime: Rising crime may discourage the use of
luxury watches, afraid of theft, affecting the brand's demand and visibility.
• Popularity of “smartwatches”: Increased demand for smart watches could
decrease the preference for traditional mechanical watches, especially among women
younger generations.
• Perception of artificial scarcity: Criticism points out that the deliberate limitation of production
creates an artificial scarcity that raises prices and raises distrust among consumers, which
which can erode the brand's reputation.
SWOT ANALYSIS OF PATEK PHILIPPE
Strengths
• Heritage and historical reputation: Founded in 1839, it is one of the oldest houses
watchmakers with uninterrupted production and, since 1932, has remained under family control
Stern, ensuring independence and long-term vision.
• Vertical production and patented innovation: Designs and manufactures all stages internally,
from design to finishing, holding more than 100 patents in complications such as
perpetual calendar, flyback chronograph and minute repeater.
• “Ultra-premium” positioning: Limited annual production (around 70,000 pieces in
2023), high prices and robust margins reinforce the exclusivity status.
• Iconic collections:
o Calatrava (1932): Example of classic elegance.
the Nautilus (1976): Sporty-luxury design designed by Gérald Genta.
o Aquanaut (1997): Appealing to a younger audience, with a composite bracelet.
• Strong appreciation in the secondary market: Worldwide auctions present Patek
Philippe at the top of the most expensive watches sold.
• Global recognition of prestige: Watches are a symbol of “status” among
collectors and brand ambassadors around the world.
• Talent retention: Specialized craftsmen with decades of experience guarantee
continuity of exclusive “know-how”.
• Restoration and certification services: Internal workshop accredited for restoration and
authentication, value legacy and increase customer trust.
Weaknesses
• Restricted production scale: Although it guarantees exclusivity, it limits the ability to
increase revenue and reach emerging segments.
• High entry price: Makes it difficult to attract beginners and professional collectors
young people.
• Dependence on central lines: Calatrava, Nautilus and Aquanaut correspond to a large
part of sales, which increases the risk in case of changing trends.
• Family governance: Despite ensuring independence, future successions can generate
uncertainties.
• Digital challenge: E-commerce and online communication strategies less
developed compared to some competitors.
• Exclusive supply of materials: Dependence on single certified suppliers
can create vulnerability in stock delays.
• Gender balance: Low proportion of women in technical departments, which limits
diverse perspectives.
• High training costs: Significant investment in the qualification of artisans, with
long periods of learning before autonomy.
Opportunities
• Growth in emerging markets: Expansion in Asia, Middle East and America
Latin, where ultra-luxury is in strong demand.
• Official “Certified Pre-Owned” program:
• Capitalize on the secondary market with guarantees and dedicated after-sales services.
• New collections and limited editions: Launch of innovative lines to attract
urban audiences and young collectors.
• Sustainability and transparency: Adoption of “Fairmined” gold, RJC certification and
ESG reports to improve image among consumers concerned about the environment
environment.
• Digital personalization: “Virtual-to-store” platforms for customizing displays,
bracelets and engravings.
• Hybrid “Smartwatches”
• Development of mechanical models with technological features
complementary.
• VIP loyalty programs
• Exclusive events and personalized experiences for high-value customers.
• Cultural partnerships
• Collaborations with museums and artistic institutions for commemorative editions and events.
Threats
• Rivalry with Audemars Piguet and Vacheron Constantin.
• Global recessions, inflation or international conflicts can reduce demand for goods
of luxury.
• Unauthorized resale and the proliferation of replicas harm the brand image and
challenge price controls.
• Generation Z and “millennials” tend to value experiences over possession of
material goods, which may affect demand for traditional mechanical watches.
• The appreciation or devaluation of major currencies (Swiss franc, euro, dollar) may
affect price competitiveness and profit margins.
• New standards for the extraction and processing of precious metals may increase costs
production and delay launches.
• Vulnerabilities in e-commerce and CRM systems can compromise data
sensitivity of customers and the manufacturing itself.
• Suspension of in-person events, fairs and closure of boutiques may reduce
sales and brand visibility.
• Criticism and campaigns suggest that deliberately limiting production creates a shortage
artificial, inflating prices and may generate distrust among consumers and
damage to the brand's reputation.
VACHERON SWOT ANALYSIS
CONSTANTIN
Strengths
• Inheritance and antiquity
• Founded in 1755, it is the oldest watchmaking house in continuous operation, with
270 years of history and tradition.
• Belongs to the Richemont Group
• Benefits from marketing, logistics and finance synergies, but preserves a high degree of
creative independence.
• “Haute horology” with manually applied finishes, “anglage”, “guilloché”,
classic engraving and enameling guarantee prestige.
• Develops complications such as “tourbillon”, minute repeater and perpetual calendar,
signed by “Poinçon de Genève”.
• Iconic collections
o Patrimony: sober lines of classical inspiration.
o Overseas: sporty-elegant with interchangeable strap.
o Historiques: reissues of emblematic models.
• Restoration Center in “Plan-les-Ouates” that takes care of historical pieces, valuing the
brand legacy.
• Superior quality certification that reinforces trust and differentiation.
• Good appreciation at auctions for rare and vintage references, sustaining brand equity.
Weaknesses
• Only produces around 30,000 pieces/year, far from Patek and AP, which may restrict
revenue growth.
• Less variety of complications and lines compared to the “Holy Trinity” competition.
• Belonging to the “Richemont Group”, although it offers advantages, can impose alignments
strategic items that do not coincide 100% with the brand identity.
• Minimum purchase value (>€15,000) limits access to new enthusiasts and older generations
young people.
• Online communication and “e-commerce” less robust than some rivals and presence in
social networks more contained.
• Compared to AP and Patek, releases fewer rare “vraiment” pieces, which reduces “Buzz” along with
of collectors.
• The strength of the Swiss franc could make prices less competitive internationally.
• Boutique network limited in number and geography, forcing customers to travel to
assistance and purchase.
Opportunities
• Expand the number of boutiques and events in China, the Middle East, India and America
Latin.
• Create an official platform for authenticated vintage watches to capture revenue and build loyalty
enthusiasts.
• Partnerships with artists, museums or art/car brands for numbered series of
high appeal.
• Augmented reality tools to virtually “try on” models and
configure customizations.
• Certification of precious metals and stones, carbon footprint reports and initiatives
environmental neutrality.
• VIP programs for annual maintenance, complimentary parts loan and reservations
anticipated releases.
• Discreetly integrate connectivity functions without losing the luxury mechanical character.
• Traveling exhibitions and publications that celebrate centuries-old milestones and pioneering spirit
watchmaker.
Threats
• Direct pressure from Audemars Piguet and Patek Philippe by the same “ultra-
premium.”
• Financial crises, inflation and political instability that slow down luxury consumption.
• Unauthorized resale and counterfeits can dilute “perceived value” and confidence in
brand.
• Generation Z and “millennials” value digital experiences and technological products in
to the detriment of mechanics.
• New laws on the extraction of precious metals and import/export barriers that
increase costs.
• Closing points of sale and postponing large watch shows could reduce
visibility and sales.
• Attacks on CRM systems, “e-commerce” and customer databases put the company at risk
sensitive information.
• Criticism about deliberate limitation of production to inflate prices can generate
discredit among consumers
03 MARKETING MIX
AUDEMARS PIGUET
Product: Strongly bets on boldness and innovation. The Royal Oak line is its icon
Absolute, mixing industrial design with artisanal finishing. Launches limited pieces, uses
materials such as ceramics, forged carbon, and focus on proprietary movements. Likes to tease
with unexpected designs and cultural “collabs”.
Price: Positioned in the “ultra-luxury” segment, but with a more “culturally
desired” than just traditional. Entrance prices are around 20–25 thousand euros,
but exclusive pieces can exceed 200 thousand. The perceived value is high, in part due to
“hype” and scarcity.
Place: Has invested in an almost exclusively direct distribution model, through
its “AP Houses” in key cities. It left many multi-brand retailers to control
better experience and positioning. Some editions are accessible only by invitation or
relationship with the brand.
Promotion: Communicates in a modern way, with a strong digital presence. Collaborate with
artists, musicians, athletes and participates in events such as “Art Basel”. The brand bets on
impactful visual narratives, behind-the-scenes content, and videos that associate the watch with
contemporary culture and performance.
PATEK PHILLIPE
Product: It is the guardian of tradition. Their watches are classic, conservative in design and
highly sophisticated in movements. Invests a lot in Grand Complications and calibers
own. Each piece is made to last for generations, without giving in to fashions. The focus is on inheritance and
technical perfection.
Price: Operates with an even higher pricing strategy, based on the idea of legacy and
investment. A Calatrava starts at 25 thousand euros, but complications and special editions
they easily rise to 500 thousand or more. It's a mark of heritage, not ostentation.
Place: Remains faithful to the traditional distribution model: authorized points of sale
highly selective and few own boutiques. The purchase is often shrouded in
formality and restricted access, reinforcing the idea of prestige and scarcity.
Promotion: Maintains a reserved and institutional tone. Its most famous campaign, “You
never actually own a Patek Philippe...”, focuses on generational value. The brand avoids celebrities,
remains discreet on social media and favors word-of-mouth among collectors.
VACHERON CONSTANTIN
Product: Focuses on artistic “savoir-faire”. The brand favors manual finishing,
enamels, engravings and other traditional watchmaking arts. Pieces such as the “Métiers d’Art” and “Les
Cabinotiers” reinforce the status of mechanical jewelry. It has a more poetic and artistic touch,
without giving up the technique.
Price: Prices are in line with haute horlogerie, although slightly below the PP in
“entry-level”. A Patrimony can start at around 18 thousand euros. At the top, the pieces “Les
Cabinotiers” easily exceed 300 thousand. The value is in art and tradition, more than
in immediate social status.
Place: Opts for a hybrid model: maintains presence in luxury retailers and boutiques
own, with increasing investment in brand experience and digital. It also offers
sales to order and service by appointment for demanding customers.
Promotion: Communicates through art and detail. “Storytelling” is centered on
heritage, technical precision and manual arts. The brand participates in events
cultural and watchmaking (such as “Watches & Wonders”) and invests in videos with a tone
inspiring and calm, unhurried, like your watches.

05 “GOLDEN CIRCLE”
The “Golden Circle” exists as a “framework” used to define how a
brand communicates.
It establishes that communication must be done from the inside out, starting with “passing”
purposes and values before promoting products or services.
This “framework then allows effectiveness in strengthening the emotional relationship between the public and
visa brand makes it communicate in a way that is “perceived” as more human and
genuine.
Since Audemars Piquet sells luxury watches that no one “needs” is important
add the greatest possible value to the brand (“perceived” or not).
The AP “Golden Circle” exists in the following form:
WHY – (The Reason for Being)
Create magnificent and complex pieces of time that transcend functionality, where each
it is an artistic expression of mastery, heritage and innovation.
This is the heart of the brand: passion, legacy and creative boldness. It's not just about watches,
it is a legacy that is worn on the wrist.
HOW – (The Single Process)
Preserving the “savoir-faire” of Swiss watchmaking through artisanal processes led by
master watchmakers who fuse tradition with innovation.
This creation method highlights rarity, exclusivity, authenticity and a human touch,
exactly what the contemporary luxury consumer values most.
WHAT – (The Offer)
Swiss watches of exceptional complexity that combine traditional watchmaking techniques with
cutting-edge innovation, each piece is a limited edition work of art.
From Royal Oak to Code 11.59, AP's offering is never just a product, it's a statement
cultural.
06 SMART OBJECTIVES
1. LinkedIn – Strengthen AP’s leadership and reputation (ToFu/MoFu)
Objective:
In 3 months, increase the number of qualified followers on LinkedIn by 1,500 by publishing
content that demonstrates that Audemars Piguet is at the top not because of luck, but because of “knowledge”
how” and work in excellent watchmaking.
2. Instagram – Increase engagement and visual brand recognition (MoFu)
Objective:
In 3 months, achieve a 25% growth in “engagement” (likes, comments and
shares) in Instagram posts, through impactful visual content that
transmit the exclusivity and innovation of Audemars Piguet, with an average frequency of 1
“post” per day.
3. YouTube – Convert qualified leads through premium and exclusive content (MoFu)
Objective:
In 3 months, launch a 6-episode premium series with John Mayer and exclusive stories from
customers (3 “brand ambassadors” and 3 “normal” customers), aimed at converting
watchmaking into high-value leads. The objective is to increase direct and
appointments for personalized consultations, visits to boutiques and private events, through
content that reinforces exclusivity and allows the capture of leads via forms or
CRM integration.
4. Facebook – Strengthen the relationship and generate trust with more mature audiences (MoFu/BoFu)
Objective:
In 3 months, increase meaningful interactions (comments + private messages) by 30%
via Messenger) with users 35+, through content that combines legacy, stories
humanities and local activations (events in boutiques, watchmaking experiences, launches
discrete).
The focus is on consolidating relational presence, stimulating private conversation and nurturing more leads
traditional content with content designed for calm, credible and emotional consumption.
07 TONE OF VOICE
LinkedIn – Sophisticated and Craftsman
Why:
Channel to showcase complexity, mastery, tradition and innovation. The audience values the process,
the heritage and intelligence behind the brand.
Tom: Intelligent, technical, human.
Example: "From Le Brassus to the world: where haute horlogerie is a human story of
patience, precision and purpose."
Instagram – Timeless and Poetic
Why:
Visual platform where emotion and lifestyle merge with the image.
Tone: Sensory, minimal in words, poetic.
Example: "It's not just a watch. It's a whisper of time, engraved in gold."
YouTube – Culturally Fluent and Contemporary
Why:
Channel for audiovisual “storytelling”, exploring intersections with art, music, design and figures
like John Mayer.
Tone: Modern, elegant, narrative.
Example: "When rhythm meets precision, every second is a note."
Facebook – Reliable, Relational and Lasting
Why:
Facebook continues to be relevant for audiences 35+, where many buyers are found
real haute horlogerie.
Tom: Serene, close, respectful and emotional. An invitation to trust and shared memory.
Tone example:
Some movements count time. Others tell stories.
WhatsApp – Exclusive, Discreet and Personal
Why:
Direct and private communication channel with high-value customers. Ideal for sharing
personalized services, scheduling experiences, after-sales assistance and exclusive previews.
Tom: Elegant, direct, human and attentive, like a whisper between those who already know each other.
Example: "Good afternoon, Mr. Victor. The Royal Oak model you requested arrived this morning.
We reserved the first one for you."

arrivals, find out about private events, or even reserve/buy a piece.
According to studies carried out with a special focus on this type of consumer, it is possible to perceive
that there is a growing trend to use WhatsApp as a shopping “hub”.
The “post-Covid” period saw brands make a “pivot” in order to meet the needs
of these consumers, who were looking for a direct and private line of access to brands 24 hours a day
per day and 7 days a week. A particularly illustrative case is that of Mercedes-Benz Turkey:
by integrating WhatsApp directly into its ads, it replaced traditional forms with
a click that immediately started a conversation with the brand. The result? 93% increase
in conversions, almost three times more qualified leads and even direct sales
in the conversation. More than convenience, it was about designing a discreet, functional channel with
human touch, exactly what modern luxury demands.
Another example of luxury that knew how to take advantage of this channel was Dolce & Gabbana Alta Moda.
During the pandemic, the brand transformed WhatsApp into a true intimate point of contact
with its “UHNW” clients. Exclusive tests began to be accompanied by
personalized video calls and chats, where choices of pieces costing tens of thousands of euros
they were done without leaving the sofa, whether on a yacht or in a country house. WhatsApp is no longer
just a tool and has become the invisible “hub” of luxury, where service
personalized and discreet reinforces the exclusivity and proximity that haute couture clients
demand.

13 EDITORIAL LINE
When we talk about editorial line we are talking about defining themes, values and type of language
that we want our content to possess in order to resonate with our target audience.
In the specific case of Audemars Piguet, I decided to create four thematic pillars that I believe are
necessary to cover everything related to this brand and which, in one way or another,
another, define it.
CONTENT PILLARS:
Products: Everything related to watches fits here, the product
final and finished.
Any mention of innovations, technologies and materials must be made in a superficial way.
in order to avoid cannibalizing interest in “posts” that fit into the next pillar (Technology),
The aim is to capture people's attention and stimulate their emotional and less rational side,
we want them to observe and desire without thinking about what makes up the watch.
Technology: This pillar’s main objective is to make the public aware of what it does
of a different Audemars Piguet watch.
From the complexity of a “Tourbillon” to the extreme scratch resistance of ceramics
passing through the double sapphire glass, we want to show that all our watches are
thought out down to the smallest detail.
History: The “History” pillar seeks to demonstrate to the public AP’s contributions to the
world of “Haute Horology” throughout its decades of existence, whether through the exhibition of
all the watches that broke barriers and made the impossible possible or through
Recognition from those, like Gerald Genta, shaped the brand to be what it is today.
Content created with this pillar in mind educates the public and reinforces authority in the sector
due to centuries-old experience.
Mundo AP: A brand with the aspirational character of Audemars Piguet must reinforce its
exclusivity and rarity of your pieces, but at the same time, if you do it too much, you end up
for making your watches less of a dream and more of a fantasy.
When transforming from dream (attainable) to fantasy (impossible), the client (or potential
customer) begins to look favorably on the competition that he thinks gives him greater
likely to purchase some of these special pieces.
In order to avoid this situation, the content developed under this pillar will show common parts
(SS Royal Oak) and uncommon (Royal Oak OpenWorked Frosted Gold) in customer hands
common (Locksmiths) and uncommon (Rappers), to be loved and used, in order to create bonds
among all the participants, who have something in common, the love for watchmaking.
This pillar seeks to show what happens to our watches when they leave the brand's possession and
make their way across the world.
Collection pieces that spend much of their time in safes or lived-in “tools” that are
passed from father to son.
